Number of hardware graphics adapters PULSE inventoried. Software adapters such as Microsoft Basic Render Driver and WARP are not counted.
Speed the adapter's fan is turning at, in revolutions per minute. A fan control percentage is a duty cycle rather than a speed, and is never published in its place.
Current graphics clock the driver reports. Boost behaviour and power policies move it continuously, so it is the platform's latest figure rather than an instantaneous measurement of the silicon.
Current video memory clock the driver reports.
Dedicated video memory still available for allocation.
Dedicated video memory installed on this adapter. System memory shared with an integrated GPU is deliberately not reported here.
Share of dedicated video memory in use, computed from used and total bytes.
Dedicated video memory currently in use across the whole system.
Temperature of the graphics processor die, as its own sensor reports it.
Hottest point measured on the graphics processor package. A separate sensor from the die temperature, typically reading higher under load, and never derived from it.
Temperature of the dedicated video memory, from its own sensor.
Share of the graphics engine's capacity in use, as the driver reports it.
Total addressable capacity of the physical device. This is the whole device, not the sum of the filesystems on it.
Total addressable capacity of the physical device. This is the whole device, not the sum of the filesystems on it.
Number of physical storage devices PULSE inventoried. Partitions, loop devices, RAM disks and device-mapper volumes are not counted as devices of their own.
Share of the device's reserve of replacement blocks that remains. This is not free space on the filesystem and not unallocated capacity: a completely full drive normally still reports 100 % spare.

Space on the filesystem that holds data, defined as total minus free blocks. Used and available do not sum to the total on filesystems that reserve blocks for the superuser.

Number of mounted filesystems PULSE inventoried. A filesystem reachable at several paths counts once; pseudo-filesystems such as proc and sysfs are not counted.
Share of the filesystem that holds data, computed from used and total bytes.
Share of the filesystem that holds data, computed from used and total bytes.
Number of network interfaces PULSE monitors. The loopback interface is deliberately excluded: it always exists and only ever carries traffic that never left this machine.
How many of the monitored interfaces currently carry a link. An adapter that is enabled but has no cable, or a radio not associated with a network, is not counted.
The inbound capacity of the link, as the driver negotiated it — not how much is flowing. A gauge rather than a fixed value because Wi-Fi and Ethernet both renegotiate.
The inbound capacity of the link, as the driver negotiated it — not how much is flowing. A gauge rather than a fixed value because Wi-Fi and Ethernet both renegotiate.
The outbound capacity of the link. Equal to the inbound figure on Ethernet; frequently different on Wi-Fi.
The outbound capacity of the link. Equal to the inbound figure on Ethernet; frequently different on Wi-Fi.
The largest payload this interface carries in a single frame. A configuration fact rather than a reading, so it is a state.
The largest payload this interface carries in a single frame. A configuration fact rather than a reading, so it is a state.
Bytes arriving at this machine per second, derived from the operating system's cumulative counters between two samples. Receive means inbound, from this machine's point of view.
Bytes arriving at this machine per second, derived from the operating system's cumulative counters between two samples. Receive means inbound, from this machine's point of view.

Inbound frames that arrived intact and were discarded anyway — a full buffer, or no protocol handler wanting them. This is a local counter and is not Internet packet loss, which PULSE does not measure.

Inbound frames that arrived intact and were discarded anyway — a full buffer, or no protocol handler wanting them. This is a local counter and is not Internet packet loss, which PULSE does not measure.

Inbound frames the interface rejected because something was wrong with them — a bad checksum, a framing error. A different counter from dropped frames, and a persistent non-zero rate usually means a cable or a driver problem.

Inbound frames the interface rejected because something was wrong with them — a bad checksum, a framing error. A different counter from dropped frames, and a persistent non-zero rate usually means a cable or a driver problem.
Packets arriving per second, unicast and non-unicast together. Zero is a real measurement: it means nothing arrived during the interval.
Packets arriving per second, unicast and non-unicast together. Zero is a real measurement: it means nothing arrived during the interval.
Bytes leaving this machine per second, derived from the operating system's cumulative counters between two samples. Transmit means outbound.
Bytes leaving this machine per second, derived from the operating system's cumulative counters between two samples. Transmit means outbound.
Outbound frames discarded before transmission, usually because a queue was full.
Outbound frames discarded before transmission, usually because a queue was full.
Outbound frames the interface failed to transmit.
Outbound frames the interface failed to transmit.
Packets leaving per second, unicast and non-unicast together.
Packets leaving per second, unicast and non-unicast together.
The inbound rate negotiated with the access point. A capacity, not traffic: a link negotiated at 400 Mbit/s carrying nothing still reports 400 Mbit/s.
The outbound rate negotiated with the access point. Frequently different from the inbound rate.

A 0–100 link quality figure, published only where the operating system computes one itself. It is never derived from the signal strength: every common dBm-to-percentage formula is arbitrary, and a number produced that way would look like a measurement while being a guess.

Received signal strength in dBm, as the radio reports it — a logarithmic scale where −40 is strong and −90 is barely usable. On a radio associated over several links, this is the strongest active link's reading; dBm values are never averaged together.

How many processes are executing on a processor or queued and ready to. Nearly every process on an idle desktop is waiting instead — for a timer, for input, for a disk — so a small number here is normal and not a sign of an idle machine. Windows reports no process-level state, so this figure is unavailable there rather than fabricated.
How many processes exist on this machine right now, including the ones PULSE cannot read the details of. A process that is refused still exists and is still counted.

Every thread of every visible process, added up. Processes whose thread count could not be read contribute nothing rather than a guess, so on a machine full of protected processes this is an understatement rather than an invention.
